questions.question: To merge changes from `feature/login` into `main`, which branch must you be currently checked out on before running `git merge`?
questions.explanation: You must always be on the RECEIVING branch (the branch you want to merge changes INTO) when executing `git merge`.

questions.question: What is a 'Fast-Forward' merge in Git?

options.A: A merge completed in under 1 second
options.B: When the target branch has no new commits since branching, Git simply moves the target pointer forward to the feature branch commit without creating an extra merge commit
options.C: A merge that skips code verification
options.D: A merge executed directly on GitHub servers

questions.explanation: If no divergent commits occurred on `main`, Git simply slides the `main` pointer forward. No new merge commit is required.

questions.question: When does Git create a '3-Way Merge Commit' instead of a fast-forward?

options.A: When both the target branch AND the feature branch have had new commits since they diverged
options.B: Only when merging 3 branches at the same time
options.C: When 3 different developers review the code

questions.explanation: When histories diverge, Git analyzes the common ancestor commit plus both branch tips to generate a new merge commit combining both lines.

questions.question: Which flag forces Git to create a merge commit even if a Fast-Forward merge was possible?
questions.explanation: `--no-ff` (no fast-forward) always creates an explicit merge commit, preserving the visual record of the branch existing.

questions.question: Which command safely deletes a local branch that has already been merged?
questions.explanation: Lowercase `-d` checks if the branch has been merged into upstream; if not, Git warns and refuses to delete.

questions.question: What does capital `-D` do in `git branch -D <branch-name>`?

options.B: Force-deletes the branch even if it contains unmerged commits

questions.explanation: `-D` is a shortcut for `--delete --force`. It deletes the branch regardless of its merge status.

questions.question: Why should you delete feature branches after they are merged into `main`?

options.A: To keep the repository tidy and prevent developers from accidentally continuing work on stale branches
options.B: Git has a maximum limit of 5 branches
options.D: Old branches slow down compile speed

questions.explanation: Deleting merged branches prevents branch proliferation and ensures everyone works from active, fresh code.

questions.question: How do you delete a remote branch on GitHub from your terminal?
questions.explanation: `git push origin --delete <branch-name>` tells GitHub to remove that branch pointer from the remote repository.

questions.question: Does deleting a merged feature branch delete the commits that were on that branch?

options.A: Yes, all commits made on that branch disappear forever
options.B: No, because the commits are now part of `main`'s history, deleting the branch pointer loses no work
options.D: Yes, unless backed up on a USB drive

questions.explanation: A branch is just a pointer. Since `main` now points to or includes those commits, deleting the feature pointer loses nothing.

questions.question: Which command shows a visual ASCII graph of branch commits and merges in your terminal?
questions.explanation: `git log --graph --oneline --all` draws a beautiful visual text branch tree showing how branches diverged and merged.
